A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same APP medical-dialogue framework and ReMeDi-based evaluation. Their text, equations, figures and tables support reliable comparison. v1 has no appendix; v2 includes readable doctor and patient questionnaires in Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments using 70 ReMeDi-derived simulated consultations, including diagnostic similarity, entropy and GPT-4o-rated communication outcomes in Section 3.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments using 100 ReMeDi-derived cases, including expert diagnostic assessments, simulated-dialogue results and communication ratings from non-medical participants.

M1.justification: The MSD-grounded symptom mapping, candidate question and response generation, Bayesian calculations, entropy-based selection and human-centric phrasing remain. v2's 'one-more step thinking' and 'Bayesian active learning' explain operations already present in v1 Section 2.4. Newly specified retrieval and prompting details do not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions use ReMeDi-derived patient simulation for medical diagnosis. Represented coverage expands from 58 diseases across 15 specialties to 72 diseases across 18 specialties. This is a limited expansion within the retained clinical task and data source; calling the simulator a new benchmark does not establish a separate dataset.

E2.justification: v1 reports generic single-turn and multi-turn LLM controls. v2 Table 1 expands the actual comparison to LLaMA-70B, Claude-3, GPT-4o, QWen-72B and DeepSeek-v3 in both interaction settings. The communication comparison also adds Claude-3, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-v3 alongside the retained real-world dialogues.

E3.justification: The evaluated sample changes from 70 to 100 cases. Embedding cosine similarity is replaced by diagnostic ratings from three biomedical experts. GPT-4o communication scoring is replaced by five non-medical participants rating 20 cases comprising 100 transcripts, with randomized model order and 1–5 scales. Relationship fostering is added as an evaluation criterion, and APP is also evaluated with QWen-72B.

E4.justification: v2 supplements the existing entropy analysis with Figure 5, comparing ranked disease probabilities at iterations 1 and 5 across three specialties. Figure 3 replaces the otitis externa case with allergic rhinitis and displays evolving disease probabilities. These extend the confidence and case analyses; neither version reports component ablations or robustness tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or inter-rater agreement. v2's rater counts describe evaluation design. Entropy and disease-probability plots concern diagnostic confidence rather than statistical uncertainty in reported performance.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports iteration-six similarity of 85.7% for APP versus 83.8% for the multi-turn baseline. v2 replaces this with expert diagnostic scores, including overall multi-turn scores of 3.59 for APP-DeepSeek-v3 versus 3.17 for DeepSeek-v3. Entropy results and communication scores also change: v2 Table 2 reports relevance of 4.48 versus 3.24 for real-world dialogues, whereas v1 reports 0.79 versus 0.82. Changed samples and scoring procedures prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The operative mathematical formulation remains unchanged: Equations (1)–(5) retain the disease distribution, joint and posterior probability calculations, entropy objective and question-selection rule. The expanded terminology and illustrative examples add explanation, without new theoretical results, proofs or substantive revisions to the calculations.

C1.justification: v2 elevates the ReMeDi-derived patient simulator into a claimed new benchmark contribution and makes transparent diagnosis through Bayesian active learning a central claim. v1 primarily foregrounds diagnostic accuracy, efficiency and accessible communication. The underlying diagnostic and human-centric claims remain, but the stated contribution scope is substantially expanded.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations absent from v1: greedy question selection may produce suboptimal sequences, guideline quality and coverage constrain applicability, and simulated consultations and transcript ratings require validation in clinical trials. Section 3.6 also develops an interpretation linking probability-rank separation and intermediate calculations to transparency and trust.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies K=5 candidate questions, 2–5 responses per question, local symptom-description retrieval, persona-only simulator access and prompting examples. Appendix A supplies detailed evaluation instruments. Conversely, v1's GPT-4o translation and English-output description and planned code-release link disappear. These are documentation and access-information changes; they do not establish changed earlier hyperparameters or actual repository availability.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises the introduction's research context and adds a dedicated related-work section covering medical dialogue fine-tuning, question asking, grounding and patient-oriented evaluation. Added discussions include Bianque, DISC-MedLLM, Mediq and Zhongjing, while several earlier online-consultation and retrieval references disappear. This materially expands positioning against relevant conversational research.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and substantial methodology passages are rewritten. APP is increasingly presented as Dr.APP, the former follow-up-question subsection becomes three separately explained stages, and patient simulation receives its own subsection. Related work, limitations and survey appendices substantially reorganize the narrative beyond the added experimental content.

P2.justification: The paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 2 is redrawn as a numbered workflow, and Figure 3 presents a different case with probability bars. Table 1 changes from an iteration-based similarity table to a model-by-specialty diagnostic comparison. Figure 5 and the human-centric comparison in Table 2 are new displays.

improvement.justification: Expert diagnostic assessments and independent non-medical participant ratings replace v1's embedding and GPT-4o proxies, substantially improving how the central clinical and communication claims are tested. Broader model comparisons, explicit survey rubrics and substantive limitations further strengthen the evidence. Removing code-release and English-processing information weakens reproducibility, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial evaluation improvements.
